entries.what_happened: Two OpenAI manuscripts, both dated 24 September 2026, which depend on each other. (1) 'Rigidity of Smooth Billiards with a Continuous Caustic Collar' (the companion, cited as NB in the other paper) proves: if a bounded, strictly convex planar domain Ω with C∞ boundary of positive curvature has a continuous physical caustic collar, meaning a homeomorphism H0 from S¹×[0,1) onto a relatively open neighbourhood A of ∂Ω in the closed table, with H0 on the zero leaf equal to ∂Ω and every positive leaf a C∞ smooth closed convex caustic, then Ω is an ellipse (circles included; the conclusion is Ω = {x : (x−c)ᵀQ(x−c) < 1} with Q symmetric positive definite). No differentiability across leaves is assumed. The proof goes through analytic boundary regularity (§2), a joint parametrization (§3), continuation and shape-lift arguments and growth-order exclusions (§4 to §7), a critical-case reduction (§8 to §9), and a sign-test contradiction for the remaining finite critical wall (§10 to §11). (2) 'Continuous Phase Foliations Create Analytic Caustic Collars' (the Phase paper) proves the same conclusion for the same class of tables under a different hypothesis: if a T-invariant open annulus U in the billiard phase cylinder contains (ℝ/Lℤ)×(0,η) for some η>0, and there is a homeomorphism H from S¹×(0,1) onto U whose leaves are essential simple closed curves each individually invariant under the billiard map, then Ω is an ellipse. Its route is to show the boundary is real analytic, to construct a jointly real-analytic family of smooth strictly convex caustics Γ_λ (0 ≤ λ ≤ λ0) whose positive leaves fill a relatively open collar of ∂Ω, and then to conclude by applying the companion's Theorem 1.2 (physical-collar rigidity). So the Phase paper replaces the companion's caustic hypothesis with a continuous invariant-curve hypothesis on a grazing annulus, and its own proof ends at the caustic collar.
entries.delivers: For the list's question (strictly convex and integrable implies ellipse), the family gives a positive answer for a near-boundary integrability notion only. If Ω is bounded, has C∞ boundary of positive curvature, and either (companion) a full neighbourhood of its boundary is continuously foliated by smooth closed convex caustics, or (Phase paper) a full grazing annulus is continuously foliated by individually invariant essential billiard-invariant curves, then Ω is an ellipse. The companion's abstract says it 'resolves the near-boundary Birkhoff conjecture in the stated smooth class'; the Phase paper says it resolves the near-boundary version 'positively in the continuous phase-foliation formulation'. Neither says it settles the Birkhoff conjecture as the list words it. Against the list's wording, the manuscripts add boundedness, C∞ smoothness and positive curvature, and they take integrability only near the boundary. The companion's hypothesis is the list's 'caustic-integrable' variant restricted to a neighbourhood of the boundary; the Phase paper's is the invariant-curve form of that variant, also near the boundary. The conclusion matches the list: ellipse, circles included. The converse is not claimed.
entries.remains: Still open if the claims are correct: (a) the general planar statement for smooth strictly convex integrable tables under the other notions of integrability, namely total integrability by non-contractible invariant curves on the whole phase cylinder (Bialy's theorem is cited, not reproved here), a first integral with nonvanishing gradient, polynomial integrability, and integrability away from the boundary; (b) tables whose boundary is only C^k or C², or that have points of vanishing curvature (the papers assume positive curvature throughout, and the Phase paper cites Mather for why grazing caustics fail when curvature vanishes); (c) unbounded domains; (d) any statement about the converse direction, which the list does not ask for. Also outside the family: higher dimensions and other billiard models, which the list does not ask about.
entries.direction: proves the conjecture for near-boundary integrability (positive answer in that class: caustic collar, or continuous invariant-curve foliation of a grazing annulus)
entries.object: No counterexample is constructed; the conclusion is that the table is an ellipse. The Phase paper constructs a jointly real-analytic family of strictly convex caustics Γ_λ that fills the collar, from a support function g(θ,λ) obtained from a joint holomorphic parametrization by implicit-function and Newton arguments. This object is not explicit: the paper gives no closed form.
entries.conditional_on: Phase paper: the final ellipse conclusion is not proved in that paper; it is deduced from the companion's Theorem 1.2 (physical-collar rigidity). Its analytic and joint steps also import from the companion, without proof, the stationary-mesh estimate (companion Lemma 2.3), the Fourier-row estimate (companion Proposition 2.4), the Newton construction of companion §3 (a version of its Proposition 3.3 is re-proved in the Phase paper), and the buffered-division and recursion lemmas (companion Lemmas 3.5 and 3.6). Companion: no external manuscript is needed. Its critical-case results are conditional inside the paper on the exclusion theorem (the 'Exclusion of the critical sequence' result in §9), which the paper proves itself.
entries.doubts: (1) The companion's critical-case reduction is explicitly conditional. Its 'Conditional angle-budget reduction' assumes that no prohibited sequence exists, and the model section says that until the exclusion proof is completed, the angle-budget and polynomial bounds conditional on it will not be used. The exclusion proof (§9) is a single paragraph that assembles earlier named results: the limiting moment law, steep and bounded contact alternatives, normal epochs, uniform witnesses, and a mesh contradiction. The finite-critical-wall case of the main proof rests on this exclusion. (2) The Phase paper's joint section says it 'follows the Newton construction of [NB, Section 3]' and cites the buffered-division and recursion lemmas from the companion instead of proving them. Its analytic section imports two estimates from the companion without proof. Its only route to the ellipse conclusion is the companion's Theorem 1.2, so the Phase paper's own proof ends at a caustic collar. (3) The Phase paper's hypothesis is weaker than the companion's (invariant curves rather than caustics). The reduction from one to the other is carried out in its geometry, analytic and joint sections, of which I read only excerpts, so I have not checked it.
